approachQuestion.prompt:
Printed factorial suffix

Return the number of trailing zero digits in the decimal representation of N!. Define 0!=1.

Example 1: N=10 -> 2.
Example 2: N=25 -> 6.
Example 3: N=0 -> 0.

Constraints and assumptions: 0 <= N <= 10^18. Return one integer. The factorial itself need not fit a machine word and must not be materialized. Choose the best time bound among the offered correct methods, then the least auxiliary storage when time ties.

options.text: Repeatedly divide a running quotient starting at N by 5 using floor division, adding every new quotient until zero.
options.feedback: Each factor of ten pairs a two with a five. Twos are plentiful in a factorial; successive quotients count the first, second and later fives.

options.text: For each integer from 1 through N, repeatedly divide a temporary copy by 5, counting every successful division.
options.feedback: It counts every factor of five correctly, but visits every factorial term instead of grouping contributions.
For N=25 this gives 5 instead of 6 because 25 contributes a second factor of five.
For N=5 this gives zero although 5!=120 has one trailing zero.

feedback.reason: Count repeated prime contributions to a factorial without constructing it.
details: Set q=N,total=0. Repeatedly replace q by floor(q/5) and add q to total until q=0. Return total.

Each factor of five pairs with an available factor of two to create a trailing decimal zero. Multiples of 25 supply a second five, of 125 a third, so add repeated quotients rather than counting only multiples of five.

“Repeatedly divide a running quotient starting at N by 5 using floor division, adding every new quotient until zero.”: Each factor of ten pairs a two with a five. Twos are plentiful in a factorial; successive quotients count the first, second and later fives.

“For each integer from 1 through N, repeatedly divide a temporary copy by 5, counting every successful division.”: It counts every factor of five correctly, but visits every factorial term instead of grouping contributions.
“Return floor(N/5).”: For N=25 this gives 5 instead of 6 because 25 contributes a second factor of five.
“Return floor(N/10).”: For N=5 this gives zero although 5!=120 has one trailing zero.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed method (divide-count). Let N be the factorial argument. Choose its tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Exact signed 64-bit integer arithmetic, casting before calculations; arithmetic and comparisons cost one unit. No arbitrary-precision operations.
Iterative method, no recursion or hashing, no input copies. Auxiliary space includes all temporary state and buffers, excluding supplied input and returned output.
Include initialization and any copying; no hidden preprocessing or cache.

options.text: O(1 + log(N + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(1 + log(N + 1)) time, O(N) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Repeated division by five gives logarithmically many scalar updates.
details: The quotient shrinks by a factor of five at every iteration. Positive N therefore takes logarithmically many divisions; N=0 returns immediately. Only a quotient and running count are kept. The sum is less than N/4 and fits the stated type.
Exact signed 64-bit integer arithmetic, casting before calculations; arithmetic and comparisons cost one unit. No arbitrary-precision operations.
Iterative method, no recursion or hashing, no input copies. Auxiliary space includes all temporary state and buffers, excluding supplied input and returned output.
“O(1 + log(N + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Correct: a divide-by-five loop with constant state.
“O(N) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This describes visiting every factorial term, not the quotient loop.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Counting higher powers of five takes an input-dependent number of steps.
“O(1 + log(N + 1)) time, O(N) auxiliary space”: No list of factors or factorial digits is stored.
